name: MCP4922-E_SL
title: Dual 8/10/12-bit voltage-output DAC with SPI interface
summary: The MCP4902, MCP4912 and MCP4922 are dual voltage-output digital-to-analog converters of 8, 10 and 12 bits, each channel with its own external reference input and a rail-to-rail buffered output with 1x or 2x gain. They are written over a 20 MHz SPI bus; an LDAC pin updates both outputs together, and a SHDN pin or a register bit shuts the channels down. One 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply, -40 °C to +125 °C, 14-pin PDIP, SOIC or TSSOP.
key_figures: 2.7 V to 5.5 V; 350 µA typ, 700 µA max at 5 V
external, 0 V to VDD unbuffered (165 kΩ, 7 pF) or 0.040 V to VDD – 0.040 V buffered
SPI modes 0,0 and 1,1, 20 MHz; LDAC, SHDN

notes: T before the dash marks tape and reel; P, SL and ST after the slash name the package.

pins.name: VDD
pins.function: Positive supply, 2.7 V to 5.5 V referred to VSS. Bypass with about 0.1 µF ceramic, with 10 µF tantalum alongside.

pins.name: CS
pins.function: Chip select, active low; while low the serial clock and data are taken in.

pins.name: SCK
pins.function: SPI serial clock; data are latched on its rising edge.

pins.name: LDAC
pins.function: Latch DAC, active low: a low level copies both input registers into the output registers so VOUTA and VOUTB change together. Tied to VSS, the outputs follow the rising edge of CS. An MCU I/O pin may drive it.

pins.name: SHDN
pins.function: Hardware shutdown, active low: a low level shuts down both DAC channels and their outputs are unavailable.

pins.name: VOUTB
pins.function: Output of DAC B, from its own amplifier; swings VSS to VDD.

pins.name: VREFB
pins.function: Reference input of DAC B, VSS to VDD; sets the voltage across the string DAC. May be tied to VDD.

pins.name: VSS
pins.function: Ground for all of the circuitry and the current return. Connect to the ground plane through a low impedance, on the analog ground where the board has one.

pins.name: VREFA
pins.function: Reference input of DAC A, VSS to VDD; sets the voltage across the string DAC. May be tied to VDD.

pins.name: VOUTA
pins.function: Output of DAC A, from its own amplifier; swings VSS to VDD.

circuits.title: Typical connection to a microcontroller
circuits.description: Two MCP49x2 parts share one SPI bus from a PIC microcontroller: its SDO feeds both SDI pins, and SCK and LDAC run to both parts, while each part has its own chip-select line (CS1 for U1, CS0 for U2). One LDAC pulse updates all four outputs at once. Each IC has 10 µF (C1) and 0.1 µF (C2) from VDD to ground. The DACs return to AVSS and the MCU to VSS. Both references and both outputs of each DAC leave the circuit as terminals.
notes: The circuit leaves SHDN and the NC pins without a connection.

circuits.title: Set point or threshold calibration
circuits.description: The DAC sets the trip point of a comparator that watches a light sensor. A photodiode from VDD into RSENSE gives a voltage on the comparator's inverting input. The DAC output is cut down by the divider R1/R2 to VTRIP on the non-inverting input, with 0.1 µF from VTRIP to ground taking out the DAC's noise and picked-up noise. The divider scales the output range down, so fine steps come from a larger VREF.
notes: The DAC is channel A of the part; its 3-wire SPI is CS, SCK and SDI. LDAC and SHDN are left without a connection.

circuits.title: Single-supply window DAC
circuits.description: A comparator threshold set by the DAC over a narrow window. R1 from the DAC output, R3 from VCC+ and R2 to VCC- meet at Vtrip, so only part of the DAC range spans the threshold and each step is finer. A sensor in series with Rsense gives the voltage the comparator's inverting input sees; 0.1 µF from Vtrip to ground filters the threshold. R2 and R3 reduce to a Thevenin source R23, V23.
notes: The DAC is channel A of the part; its 3-wire SPI is CS, SCK and SDI. LDAC and SHDN are left without a connection.
The comparator runs from VCC+ and VCC-; the supply at the upper end of the sensor is not named.

circuits.title: Digitally controlled bipolar voltage source
circuits.description: An op amp turns the single-supply DAC output into a bipolar voltage. R3/R4 scale and offset the DAC output to VIN+, filtered by 0.1 µF; R1 from VREF and R2 in feedback set the gain and pull the output below ground at low codes. The values are those of the worked design: ±2.05 V in 1 mV steps from a 12-bit part with VREF = 4.1 V.
notes: The DAC is channel A of the part; its 3-wire SPI is CS, SCK and SDI. LDAC and SHDN are left without a connection.
R4 may go to VREF instead of ground, or a pull-up to VREF may replace it, for a higher offset.

circuits.title: Bipolar voltage source with selectable gain and offset
circuits.description: Both channels of one dual DAC drive an op amp: DACA through R1 into the inverting input sets the gain term, DACB through R3 into the non-inverting input sets the offset. R4 to VCC- and the optional R5 to VCC+ shift the non-inverting node (with R4 and R5 both fitted it is a bipolar window DAC); 0.1 µF filters it and R2 closes the loop. Used in multiplier mode it can linearise a sensor with varying slope and offset.
notes: DACA and DACB are the two channels of one MCP4902, MCP4912 or MCP4922; the 3-wire SPI is CS, SCK and SDI. LDAC and SHDN are left without a connection.

circuits.title: Double-precision DAC with MCP4922
circuits.description: The two outputs of one MCP4922 are summed by a divider into a voltage follower: DACB (coarse) through R2 = 100 Ω and DACA (fine) through R1 = 100 kΩ, so DACA moves the output by about 1/1000 of its own step and can make up DACB's DNL error. With R1 >> R2 the result reaches about 1 µV steps over 0 V to 4.1 V, though the transfer is not exactly linear. 0.1 µF filters the summing node.
notes: DACA and DACB are the two channels of one MCP4922; the 3-wire SPI is CS, SCK and SDI. LDAC and SHDN are left without a connection.
R1 = 100 kΩ and R2 = 100 Ω are the worked values for 1 µV steps.

circuits.title: Digitally controlled current source
circuits.description: An op amp and an NPN transistor make the DAC voltage into a load current. The op amp holds the emitter, across RSENSE, at VOUT, so the collector current through the load is set by VOUT and RSENSE. A smaller RSENSE wastes less power but gives coarser current steps; the window divider of the window DAC circuit can win the resolution back. A capacitor filters VOUT.
notes: The DAC is channel A of the part; its 3-wire SPI is CS, SCK and SDI. LDAC and SHDN are left without a connection.
The capacitor on VOUT carries no value.

circuits.title: Multiplier mode in a motor control loop
circuits.description: The DAC works as a multiplier inside a motor speed loop. An op amp compares the set speed VRPM_SET with the measured speed VRPM, with ZFB as its feedback, and its output becomes the DAC's VREF; the DAC scales it by Dn/2^N times the gain. A second op amp and an NPN transistor turn VOUT into motor current through Rsense. VRPM is taken from the motor.
notes: The DAC is channel A of the part; its 3-wire SPI is CS, SCK and SDI. LDAC and SHDN are left without a connection.
The supplies of U2 are not given, the motor supply is not named, and VRPM is measured from the motor.

operation.text: MCP4902, MCP4912 and MCP4922 are dual voltage-output DACs of 8, 10 and 12 bits, built as resistor strings, which gives low DNL and fast settling. Each channel has its own external reference input, an optional reference buffer and a rail-to-rail output amplifier with 1x or 2x gain. They run from one 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply over -40 °C to +125 °C. The MCP4801/4811/4821 and MCP4802/4812/4822 (internal 2.048 V reference) and MCP4901/4911/4921 (external reference, single channel) have similar AC and DC performance.

The bus is SPI, modes 0,0 and 1,1, write only: nothing can be read back. A write takes CS low, clocks 16 bits into SDI on the rising edges of SCK (four configuration bits, then 12 data bits, most significant first) and takes CS high, which loads the selected channel's input register. Clocks after the 16th are ignored; if CS rises before 16 clocks the write is dropped, and nothing is taken in while CS is high. The interface also suits Microwire ports.

Each channel has an input register and an output (DAC) register. A low level on LDAC moves both input registers into the output registers, so both outputs change together. With LDAC tied to VSS the interface needs only three lines and the output changes when CS rises after a valid 16-clock write.

The BUF bit chooses for each channel whether VREF goes through the input buffer. Buffered, the input impedance is very high and the range and bandwidth are slightly limited. Unbuffered (BUF = 0) is the default, taking 0 V to VDD with about 165 kΩ and 7 pF.

Each output is buffered by a low-power precision CMOS amplifier with low offset and noise that swings close to both rails and is stable into large capacitive loads, so VOUT can serve as a programmable reference. GA = 1 selects 1x and GA = 0 selects 2x, the default. Gain 2x lowers the multiplier-mode bandwidth. Most loads need no buffer after the output.

The POR circuit watches VDD. Below VPOR (2.0 V typical) the DACs are held in reset; at power-up the outputs are high impedance (SHDN bit = 0, about 500 kΩ) until a valid write reaches either DAC register and LDAC is below its low threshold. Whether a supply dip causes a reset depends on its depth below VPOR and its duration; 0.1 µF as close as possible to VDD adds immunity.

Each channel can be shut down by its SHDN bit, or both by the SHDN pin. A shut-down channel turns most of its circuits off, gives no output and ties VOUT internally to about 500 kΩ. The serial interface stays active, so a write can wake it. A pin shutdown turns the POR circuit off; a software shutdown leaves it on. The channel stays off until SHDN goes high or a write with SHDN bit = 1 is latched. Coming out of shutdown the output settles within 10 µs, longer than the 4.5 µs normal settling.

INL is the largest gap between an actual and an ideal code transition after offset and gain errors are taken out, using the two end points 0x000 and 0xFFF; positive means transitions late, negative early. DNL is the spread of code widths about the ideal 1 LSb; zero means all codes have the ideal 1 LSb width. Offset error is the output at code zero. Gain error is the departure from the ideal full-scale output, VREF - 1 LSb, without the offset error. 1 LSb is the ideal step between adjacent codes.

A signal on VREF is scaled by the code: in 1x gain it is attenuated by D/2^n; on a 12-bit part in 2x gain codes below 2048 attenuate and codes above 2048 amplify. Unbuffered the input range is 0 V to VDD, buffered it is nearly rail to rail, and the bandwidth is above 400 kHz. Uses include programmable gain or attenuation and motor control loops; the DAC gives far finer gain steps than a typical programmable-gain amplifier.

Use two bypass capacitors in parallel, 0.1 µF ceramic and 10 µF tantalum, within 4 mm of the VDD pin. Keep the supply as free of noise as you can; with separate analog and digital supplies, VDD and VSS belong on the analog plane.

Inductively picked-up transients and noise from digital switching spoil signal integrity. A multilayer board with a low-inductance ground plane, inputs and outputs kept apart and proper decoupling gives the best results; harsh surroundings may call for shielding. Breadboards and wire-wrapped boards do not suit low-noise work.

With VREF = 4.096 V the MCP4922's 4096 steps are 1 mV each; finer steps need a lower reference or a divider on the output. A divider lets a larger VREF be used when a very low reference would be too noisy or is not available; a bypass capacitor on the divider output is important for filtering. Example: 0.8 V of bias range in about 200 µV steps comes from VREF of 0.82 V or a divider. When calibration uses only a small part of the range, a window divider narrows the range around the threshold.
For tiny sensor signals, store the DAC setting found under known sensor conditions to cancel the amplifier's offset error.
